citations.translation: when in a month wherein at the beginning of the month of Nisan Saturn rises from the left while the Sun appears to have set

citations.sourceExpanded: Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft
citations.translation: [rendered "Parhelion" but the text corresponds to the Mandaic omen here cited]

notes.text: In Indian astrology Saturn is considered the son of the Sun (so the notes in Drower's Book of the Zodiac p. 138). Furlani in ZDMG cited by and followed by LS takes the meaning to be a parhelion. The Syriac and Mandaic passages clearly refer to the same phenomenon -- indeed the text traditions are clearly related. The Mandaic passage could describe something like a parhelion, but we take it to be the son of the Sun, i.e. Saturn. However, in the Syriac of Bar Hebraeus, the expression "daughters" of the Sun, ܒܢ̈ܬ ܫܡܫܐ, clearly refers to parhelions (BHCandBak [116]4ff.).

notes.text: See also s.v. byt, byny. Note that in LJLA it occurs only in TargProv and one time each in TgPsJ and MegAntioch where the meaning is clearly "among". This is the plural form of byt prep., and in many Syriac texts there is a clear distinction between the use of byt for "between" and bynt (usually with syāmē!) for "among", hence we have here separated the two. Elsewhere the two may be used in close context simply for variation. In Mandaic this form appears to be used in complementary distribution with binia when used with pronominal suffixes.

notes.text: See also s.v. pqʕh. It is important to understand the difference in meaning between the terms "valley," "plain," and "mountain" in regions such as the Near East and the American West and the way they are typically used in European/American languages. A "valley" in such regions is often a vast flat "plain" between distant mountain ranges, whereas the term for "mountain" (e.g. Akkadian šadû) can correspond to the word "plateau" or "plain" when viewed from the other side, while in Europe one expects mountains to have peaks and valleys to be the deep areas between them. For a possible semantic development in JBA see s.v. byqytɁ n.f.

notes.text: This word is used in both major meanings "structure/house" and "place, location" in many compounds. Here, in contrast with many previous writers, we have separated out as independent lemmas only those meanings wherein a distinct meaning has developed, especially those verified by attestation in several dialects. Thus examples like by twryn and by tbn, "cattle barn" and "straw shed," are not considered to be lemmas unless there is a distinct difference in meaning between the "compound" using the construct state on the first word and the same expression using the d_ genitive on the second word. But the form binat with pronominal suffixes is well attested. It is often difficult to distinguish between this usage and the homophonous construct of "house" in Syriac; hence the origin of the usage as a variant of byn and bynt. N.B.: The decision to list one or another of these collocations as a separate lemma is not always a straightforward one. For the meaning "with" do not confuse instrumental b_ with locative ʕm. in some LJLA mss. one finds a form בי, both as an independent and proclitic before the third person pronoun in the sense "in that one". This is to be seen not as based on the JBA form of בין, but rather a real phonological development from bhāhī -> bayhī, etc. The JBA form, on the other hand, is surely responsible for the scribal tendency to spell it as a separate word. In any case this usage is to be kept separate from those instances where the yodh is a simple vowel letter.
